75.0.s.en: (1) Glorifying God for His justice and His power

75.0.0.en: 1- Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare.

75.0.1.en: 1- The Psalm begins with thanksgiving to God, and repeats the word "we give thanks" to show the heart's attachment to God, and its thanks to Him for His many works with His children.

75.0.2.en: 2- The wonders of God on earth with His children made Him near to their hearts, and they were bound to Him as a God of their own, and therefore they glorify Him and give thanks to Him.

75.1.0.en: 2- "For I appoint a set time; I judge uprightly.

75.1.1.en: 1- God speaks and says to those who cry out to Him, that He may take vengeance on the wicked, that He has appointed a set time for their destruction, and He now gives them an opportunity to repent. And He judges uprightly, so He rewards the righteous, and is long-suffering toward the wicked, that perhaps they may repent, but if they do not repent He will punish them and destroy them. He has also appointed a set time for the whole world at which He will judge it, which is the great Day of Judgment, and He now gives an opportunity to the righteous to be approved before Him, and to the wicked to turn back from their sins.

75.1.2.en: 2- He reassures His children who await His salvation that He has appointed a set time for the salvation of mankind by Christ the Redeemer, and that all the words of the prophets will be fulfilled in Christ, so He asks His children to await His salvation with faith, and even if they die in hope, Christ will lift them up from Hades to Paradise after He completes the redemption.

75.2.0.en: 3- The earth and all its inhabitants melt. I have weighed its pillars. Selah.

75.2.1.en: 1- God assures those who are hasty for His judgment that the earth will melt and come to an end, it and all its inhabitants, and that is on the Day of Judgment, and by its inhabitants he means earthly people, occupied with the lusts of the world, but God is long-suffering toward these earthly people that perhaps they may repent.

75.2.2.en: 2- He reassures the righteous who ask for the speed of His judgment that He is the Creator of the earth and its Ruler, and He is the One who weighed its pillars; for they used to believe anciently that the earth was fixed on pillars, so what is meant by the pillars is stability. And God knows the extent of the stability of this earth, and when He will end this stability, that is, on the Day of Judgment, and the earth and all material things will change.

75.2.3.en: 3- Since God judges uprightly, the earthly, sensual people fear and melt trembling, but would that their fear were turned into repentance and return to God.

75.2.4.en: 4- He ends these three verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditation on our God, the Controller of all, and Ruler of our life, that we may be reassured and be occupied with His love until He takes us to Himself in His heavenly Kingdom.

75.2.5.en: When you accustom yourself to thanking God you feel His nearness to you, and He also reveals Himself to you, so that your heart clings to Him and rejoices, and your thanks, your thanksgiving and your praise increase.

75.3.s.en: (2) A warning to the wicked of the wrath of the Lord

75.3.0.en: 4- I said to the boasters, Do not boast; and to the wicked, Do not lift up the horn.

75.3.1.en: The writer of the Psalm calls to the wicked, and warns them against continuing to resist the Lord; this is a divine warning from God on the tongue of the writer of the Psalm so that the wicked do not persist in their wickedness, but repent and return to God. And he warns them of two things:

75.3.2.en: 1- Pride, which he likens to the wild animal's lifting its horn and getting ready to resist and fight in defense of its evil.

75.3.3.en: 2- Stubbornness, which he likens to the animal that stiffens its neck so as not to submit to the one who leads it on the way, for it refuses obedience and submission.

75.3.4.en: The insistence of the wicked on pride and stubbornness keeps them in constant distance from God, and consequently they walk in the way of destruction.

75.4.0.en: 6- For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the wilderness of the mountains. 7- But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.

75.4.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm completes his speech about the wicked in his warnings to them, and tells them to fear God only; because He alone is the Judge who rewards the righteous and lifts them up, or puts down the wicked and punishes them.

75.4.2.en: 2- He asks the wicked to take into account: a- Let not people coming from the east, or the west, or from the wildernesses amid the mountains frighten you, that is, do not fear all men.

75.4.3.en: b- Fear God alone, from whom there is no escape, whether in the east, or the west, or even in the wildernesses among the mountains.

75.4.4.en: c- Do not pretend and please the people who are in any place.

75.5.0.en: 8- For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.

75.5.1.en: The writer of the Psalm shows God's punishment of the wicked, and likens it to a cup in the hand of the Lord, and we note in this cup several things:

75.5.2.en: 1- That its wine is "fermented", that is, strong in effect, so whoever drinks it becomes drunk with it, that is, the divine wrath is severe, and strong in its effect on the wicked.

75.5.3.en: 2- "Full", that is, its wine is plentiful, so the wrath of God will pour out abundantly on the wicked, to each according to his evil, that perhaps they may repent, and if they refuse chastening nothing awaits them but destruction.

75.5.4.en: 3- "A mixed drink", that is, it is a mixture of different kinds of wine so that its effect is stronger, and it means that the divine wrath will have varied punishments; so that its effect is severe, and pricks the wicked and distresses them that perhaps they may repent.

75.5.5.en: 4- "He poureth out of the same": God will pour out from the cup of His wrath on the wicked according to their evil; that they may forget the pleasure of lusts, and return to Him, and awake from their heedlessness.

75.5.6.en: 5- "The dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them": the dregs of the wine (the sediment) is what is at the bottom of the cup, and sucking and drinking it has a stronger effect and is more painful, and it means that the Lord in the end shows His wrath severely to the wicked as a last opportunity for repentance.

75.5.7.en: And by "sucks it" he means that he drinks it to the end and not a drop remains of it, that is, that the wicked who insist on their wickedness, God will give them complete wrath which they drink to the end in the hope that they may repent.

75.5.8.en: When you meet an affliction, know that God is alerting you by it to return to Him, and He does not want your destruction, but because of your immersion in evil He was compelled to awaken you strongly, that you may return to His embrace.

75.6.0.en: 9- But I will declare for ever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.

75.6.1.en: 1- After the writer of the Psalm has spoken of the punishment of the wicked he returns to himself, and looks at God, and his heart is filled with joy at His love and His tenderness toward His children, so his heart is quieted and he enjoys fellowship with God.

75.6.2.en: 2- From the greatness of the writer's joy he began to sing and praise God, and tell of the work of God in him and preach to all around him, and draw those far away, in addition to establishing the righteous.

75.7.0.en: 10- All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted. Cut off (a'dab): break.

75.7.1.en: 1- He closes the Psalm with the declaration of the strength of the righteous, for the righteous by the power of God breaks the power of the wicked which seems to dominate on earth, but the righteous in his quietness and reliance on God triumphs and lives in peace.

75.7.2.en: 2- In heaven, that is, the Kingdom, all the powers of evil are broken so that they no longer exist, and are cast into eternal torment, while the righteous receives very great power, which he expresses by horns, and not one horn. So the righteous lifts his head with strength and rejoices for ever, as the animal lifts its head and its horn is raised, declaring its strength.

75.7.3.en: If you look to Christ your heart is filled with joy, then you praise Him, and so you remain in this joy, and can then preach joy to others, and lead them to the spiritual life.

75.7.5.en: To the chief Musician on stringed instruments (Neginoth), a Psalm of Asaph, a song. "In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel" (v. 1). Introduction:

75.7.6.en: 1- Its writer: a- Asaph, as appears from the title, and he is the chief of the singers in the days of David.

75.7.7.en: b- There is another opinion that its writer is David, and that Asaph is the one who sang it.

75.7.9.en: a- After David's victory over the Philistines in the valley of Rephaim (2 Sam 5:17-25).

75.7.10.en: b- On the occasion of the enthronement of one of the kings, or at one of the feasts of the children of Israel.

75.7.11.en: c- After a great victory over the enemies, and some see that it is a prophecy about the victory over Sennacherib king of Assyria.

75.7.12.en: 3- This Psalm is sung accompanied by a stringed instrument called Neginoth (stringed instruments).

75.7.13.en: 4- This Psalm is considered a "song", that is, praise of God who gave His people victory over their enemies, and thanks to Him.

75.7.14.en: 5- This Psalm resembles the preceding Psalm in that their purpose is to show God as the just Judge of the whole earth.

75.7.15.en: 6- This Psalm is among the group of songs of Zion which speak of Jerusalem the holy city, and of this group are Psalms (48, 87).

75.7.16.en: 7- This Psalm is suitable for every person, when he triumphs in any spiritual war, to repeat it to thank God who supported him and gave him victory in his life over sin.

75.7.17.en: 8- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks of Christ who came from the tribe of Judah, victorious over Satan (vv. 1, 3).

75.7.18.en: 9- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

76.0.0.en: 1- In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel.

76.0.1.en: 1- God is known among His people who believe in Him, who know Him not as a name only, but as One acting in their lives and leading their journey. He is known in Judah, the tribe from which the kings came, David and his descendants, and known among all the tribes of the children of Israel; and if the nations have heard of Him, yet He is known by experience among those who believe in Him.

76.0.2.en: 2- God has been known from eternity; because He created the world and ordered it, and the life of man, but He declared Himself and became known by His Incarnation in Bethlehem, in the tribe of Judah, and among all the Jews in the tribes of Israel, and became known in the lives of His children in the New Testament, where He revealed His secrets to them, because they loved Him with all their hearts.

76.0.3.en: 3- God is great in Himself, and perfect, but His people Israel knew Him through His care for them, and His great works in them, which made them triumph over their enemies, such as their triumph over Sennacherib.

76.1.0.en: 2- In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion.

76.1.1.en: Salem: its meaning is peace, and what is meant is the city of Jerusalem, that is, the city of peace.

76.1.2.en: Zion: the most important of the five mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built. The name Zion is used to express Jerusalem.

76.1.3.en: 1- God settles and rests in Salem, that is, peace, for He rejects sin and disturbance, and He also settles in Zion, that is, in the midst of His people who believe in Him, and declares His greatness and His glory to them.

76.1.4.en: 2- The tabernacle of God which is in Jerusalem is the Tabernacle of Meeting by which He overshadows His people, and cares for them because of His dwelling in their midst. This happened in the days of David, and afterward the tabernacle became the Temple of Solomon. And in the fullness of time He presented the true tabernacle in Jerusalem, which is His Cross on which He died for the salvation of mankind.

76.2.0.en: 3- There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah.

76.2.1.en: The bright bows (al-qisiy al-bariqa): the bows (qisiy) is the plural of bow (qaws) and bright (bariqa) means gleaming.

76.2.2.en: The shield (al-mijann): it is the large buckler, and the buckler is a defensive implement consisting of a piece of wood with a loop at the back into which the soldier puts his hand, and moves the buckler in front of his head and body to protect him from the arrows of the enemy.

76.2.3.en: 1- There in Jerusalem, or among His people who believe in Him and hold fast to peace, God declared His glory, and gave them victory over their enemies whatever their weapons were; whether bows and gleaming arrows, or swords, or any defensive implements they had, all this God broke. That is, the enemy cannot stand before the power of God, and this indeed happened before Jerusalem with the army of Sennacherib, and then at the Cross when Christ bound Satan.

76.2.4.en: 2- At the end of these three verses there is the word "Selah", which is a musical pause for meditation on the greatness of God and His power.

76.2.5.en: If you meditate on the power of God, the fear of Him stirs in your heart, and at the same time you are reassured because He protects you from all the wars of the demons, so you remove your sins from you and live in peace, occupied with His love, and not disturbed by any troubles that surround you.

76.3.s.en: (2) The glory of God and His power

76.3.0.en: 4- Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey. 5- The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands.

76.3.1.en: Their sleep (sinatuhum): the beginning of their sleep, when their sleep is deep.

76.3.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm speaks to God and says to Him that You are greater and more splendid than all the great ones of the world, whom he likens to mountains, and those able to plunder and rob others, that is, they have great power and authority. Perhaps here he means the Assyrians in the days of Sennacherib.

76.3.3.en: 2- The writer of the Psalm describes the great ones of the world, that is, the Assyrians, as having, instead of plundering others, slept a deep sleep, and lost their ability to do anything, for he says they "found not their hands". By all this he means how the angel of the Lord killed them, because they besieged Jerusalem, and in pride transgressed against the name of the Lord. And so everyone who defies God, if he thinks himself victorious and triumphant, is defeated and becomes the spoil of God, and of His children.

76.3.4.en: 3- What is meant by the mountains of prey may be the demons, since they are great in their power like mountains, but they use their greatness in evil, for they want to plunder the purity and righteousness of the children of God, but by His power His children were able to trample the demons, and make them lose their ability to act, so they were silent and still like sleepers, and the children of God will plunder the demons, taking their places in heaven which became empty by their fall, so they enjoy in the Kingdom inexpressible glories.

76.4.0.en: 6- At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep.

76.4.1.en: Cast into a dead sleep (yusabbakh): sleeps a deep sleep.

76.4.2.en: 1- God's rebuke of the proud, such as Pharaoh and all his army, as these enemies slept with their horses and horsemen in the bottom of the Red Sea; that is, they died, because they spoke arrogantly against God and His people.

76.4.3.en: 2- Christ our God on the Cross rebuked Satan and all his power, which is symbolized by the horse and the horsemen, which is the strongest ancient military force, and bound Satan, and brought out Adam and his sons, and brought them up from Hades to Paradise.

76.4.4.en: 3- On the Day of Judgment God, that is, the God of Jacob, will rebuke all the powers of evil symbolized by the horse and the horsemen, that is, the demons and all the wicked, and cast them into eternal torment.

76.5.0.en: 7- Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry? 8- Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, 9- When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah.

76.5.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm declares the greatness and awesomeness of God, in whose hand is all authority, and consequently no one can stand before Him, but God issues His judgments against him from heaven, and they fear and tremble, for He is long-suffering, but He is just, so He judges the wicked, and sentences them to destruction, as He did with Pharaoh and all his army when He drowned them in the Red Sea, and with the Philistines who were defeated before David, and likewise with Moab and the children of Ammon and Edom and Aram in the days of David. And at the same time He keeps and saves His meek children who believe in Him, as He saved His people in the days of Moses and Joshua, and in all generations when they held fast to His commandments.

76.5.2.en: 2- The awesomeness of God and the fear of Him appear clearly on the Day of Judgment when all the wicked are terrified before Him, and keep silent, since there is no opportunity for repentance or resistance, and He casts them into destruction, but the meek He saves and glorifies in His Kingdom.

76.5.3.en: 3- These verses end with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditation on the greatness of God and His authority, so that all our hearts fear Him and keep away from every sin.

76.6.0.en: 10- Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou gird upon thee.

76.6.1.en: Gird upon thee (tatamantaq biha): He wears it as a girdle (mintaqa), which is what is worn on the waist and downward.

76.6.2.en: 1- The wrath of man praises God in four cases:

76.6.3.en: a- The holy wrath of man, that is, his rejection of the evil around him, so he praises and thanks and glorifies God, as Phinehas the priest did, who killed the fornicators and cleansed the house of God (Num 25:7, 8).

76.6.4.en: b- The wrath of the wicked man which God turns to good, such as the brothers of Joseph who were angry with him, and sold him as a slave, and God turned that to good, and raised him to the throne of Egypt; to store up wheat, and preserve the life of his father and his brothers, and all the world around him.

76.6.5.en: c- The wrath of man when he suffers from God's chastenings of him, but he accepts afterward, and endures these pains with contentment, so they are turned in the end to his good, and he receives a place in eternity, and he praises God, like Job the righteous.

76.6.6.en: d- The wrath of man against himself if he falls into sin, so he repents of it and praises God, as David did when the prophet Nathan alerted him to his sin.

76.6.7.en: 2- The remainder of man's wrath God girds upon Himself, and he means here the wrath of the wicked, so God is long-suffering toward them, but continues to chasten them that perhaps they may repent. And if they insist on sin God punishes them with destruction, as God struck Pharaoh and the Egyptians with the ten plagues, and in the end when they refused to submit to Him He drowned them in the Red Sea.

76.6.8.en: 3- The wrath of man in its strongest form was against Christ, whom the Jews insulted, and then crucified, and God turned their wrath into a salvation offered to all mankind, and it is the greatest praise that rises to heaven, and which all the believers enjoy, while the remainder of the wrath God girds upon Himself, and with it chastens the wicked throughout the generations. But if they do not believe and repent He casts them into eternal torment.

76.6.9.en: If God is great and awesome, then, O my soul, you should repent every day, and keep away from sin by every means, and live for Him, and not be troubled, for He is the Possessor of authority, and no one stands before Him, so do not be disturbed any more by the changes of life, or the threats of men; because God is able to protect you in all circumstances.

76.7.0.en: 11- Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared.

76.7.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm calls all those around God, who love His name, to worship Him faithfully, and to vow vows to God, and pay them, that is, that their hearts cling to God, who leads all their lives, and to bring Him presents which are their repentance and their love and their prayers and their service. And they bow down before our awesome God, who was crucified on the Cross for our redemption and salvation, and who is awesome in His Resurrection, and in all His power and His work with us.

76.7.2.en: 2- Our awesome God is the Judge on the Day of Judgment, to whom those who believe in Him bring their presents, which are their faith, and their faithfulness, and their virtues, and all the works of mercy they have done. And the common vow that every believer needs is to dedicate his heart to God, and believe in Him, and live for Him.

76.8.0.en: 12- He shall cut off the spirit of princes: he is terrible to the kings of the earth.

76.8.1.en: 1- God has authority over all men, so however great the rulers and kings of the earth become before Him, their spirits are in the grasp of His hand, and He cuts them off when He wishes, as fruit is gathered from a tree, such as the death of Herod, for the worms ate him while he was alive, and the death of Belshazzar the Babylonian king who grew proud and drank wine from the vessels of the house of the Lord (Dan 5:3), and consequently we are not disturbed by the domination of men and their persecutions of us, for their life is temporary, and they quickly return to the dust from which they were taken.

76.8.2.en: 2- God is awesome to every spiritual person who rules over himself, controlling his thoughts and his words and his conduct, and lives for God, indeed God reigns over his heart, so he lives reassured and hopes for eternal life.

76.8.3.en: Cling to God who loved you, and died for you, and care about worshiping Him in many prayers and fasts, for they are very precious in His sight. In this you hold fast to His commandments and submit to Him, and He reigns over your heart for ever. God the Savior of His people: "To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, a Psalm of Asaph. I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me" (v. 1). Introduction:

76.8.4.en: 1- Its writer: a- Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of the prophet David, and he is of the tribe of Levi, and he headed all the companies of singers at the official feasts.

76.8.5.en: b- There is an opinion that its writer is Jeduthun, who is also a leader of the singers under Asaph, and is also called Ethan the Ezrahite.

76.8.6.en: 2- It is considered a prophecy about a period in which the people of God will suffer pains and the feeling of God's distance from them, which is the period of the captivity. And some see that it is a prophecy about the period before the reign of King Josiah, when the people went away from God in the days of the two kings Manasseh and Amon.

76.8.7.en: 3- This Psalm resembles the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk (Hab 3), and it is likely that Habakkuk quoted from this Psalm, or was influenced by it; therefore this resemblance appeared in his prayer.

76.8.8.en: 4- This Psalm focuses on the wonderful work of God in the crossing of the Red Sea in the days of Moses (Exodus 14, 15).

76.8.9.en: 5- This Psalm is suitable for every person who suffers affliction and God's distance from him, so that he remembers God's former works with him and with His people, and his heart is reassured and his hope in Him is established.

76.8.10.en: 6- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
